w: Thatched-roof ryokan founded in the Edo era, oldest of seven inns scattered through Nyuto Onsenkyo's beech forest. Four distinct springs feed its wooden tubs, from milky shirayu to dark kuroyu, pooling in a mixed-gender outdoor bath that steams above the snow. Feudal lords once came here to take the cure.
s: Edo-era ryokan with milky mountain baths
why: Widely ranked Japan's most atmospheric onsen retreat

w: Three-storey wooden bathhouse built in 1894 over a spring cited in eighth-century chronicles as one of Japan's oldest, once visited by emperors and princes. Its turreted facade, tiled soaking rooms and a mikoyu chamber reserved for imperial guests reputedly inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away.
s: Japan's storied 1894 bathhouse, oldest spring
why: National Important Cultural Property, among Japan's oldest onsen

w: Steam rises over Yubatake, the wooden-troughed 'hot water field' at the town centre where scalding sulfuric spring water is channelled and cooled before reaching the bathhouses. Kusatsu has topped Japan's onsen-town rankings for decades; bathers still perform yumomi, paddling the water with long boards by hand.
s: Japan's perennial top-ranked onsen town
why: Repeatedly voted Japan's number-one hot spring resort

w: Eight scalding geothermal pools, too hot to bathe in, are toured instead as a spectacle: cobalt-blue Umi Jigoku, blood-red Chinoike Jigoku, and a crater of grey mud that plops and belches. Beppu itself pumps out more hot-spring water than anywhere else on earth, feeding thousands of onsen across the city.
s: Boiling 'hell' pools, too hot to enter
why: Japan's most extreme geothermal spectacle, highest onsen output

w: Built by volunteers in 1923 to teach a seafaring nation to swim, this half-natural, half-concrete pool sits walled into a narrow valley under Eyjafjallajokull, fed by a hot spring on the hillside. It was Iceland's largest pool until 1936; unheated changing sheds and mossy stone walls remain untouched since.
s: 1923 pool built into a volcano's shadow
why: One of Iceland's oldest and most photographed hidden pools

w: A trail through Steam Valley climbs past hissing fumaroles and bubbling mudpots to Klambragil, a river warmed by geothermal runoff to soaking temperature. Wooden platforms and a duckboard path let bathers wade in and drift downstream; unlike Iceland's built lagoons, entry is free and the water is entirely wild.
s: Free wild river, warm enough to swim in
why: Iceland's best-known free hike-in hot river bathing spot

area: Los Rios Region, Villarrica National Park
w: Twenty slate-lined pools step down a forested ravine, linked by a red-stained wooden footbridge heated from beneath by the thermal channel it follows. Architect German del Sol carved the complex from more than 60 natural springs emerging at 80C, cooled to a soakable 45C amid ferns and native coigue trees.
s: 20 slate pools threaded through a ravine
why: Landmark of thermal-spa architecture, widely called Chile's best

w: Reachable only by boat across the Ventisquero fjord, stone pools sit at the waterline where hot spring runoff meets the tide, framed by rainforest and glacier-topped peaks. The water carries magnesium, chromium and zinc from source temperatures near 80C, tempered to around 40C by the time it reaches the pools.
s: Fjord-side pools reached only by boat
why: Patagonia's most remote and scenic thermal bathing spot

area: Guanacaste, near Rincon de la Vieja
w: Fed by eight springs along a volcanic gorge near Miravalles, a mile of naturally hot river runs cool at one end and near-scalding at the other, letting bathers pick their own temperature among rock pools. Stone stairways descend into the deep canyon, with volcanic mud banks free for a self-applied facial.
s: A mile of self-mixing volcanic hot river
why: Rare thermal river you can walk and choose your own temperature

w: A milky-blue thermal river cuts through a desert canyon in the Sierra Madre foothills, spilling from a steaming cave you can wade shoulder-deep into past hanging bats. Terraced infinity pools cling to the cliffside above, fed by more than 30 hot springs at roughly 35C, with a suspension bridge crossing the gorge.
s: Milky-blue river pouring from a hot cave
why: One of Mexico's most visually striking natural hot spring canyons

w: Springs emerging at up to 80C beside the Parvati River cook communal langar meals for pilgrims at the adjoining Sikh gurdwara and Hindu Ram temple, both tied to a Puranic legend of Shiva and Parvati's lost earring. Bathhouses along the riverbank offer the scalding water free to travellers and sadhus alike.
s: Sacred spring that cooks pilgrims' meals
why: Himalayan pilgrimage hot spring shared by Hindus and Sikhs since the 15th century

w: A turquoise, sulfur-choked pool steams to near-boiling behind a safety fence at the head of Beitou's spring network, one of only two green-sulfur hot springs recorded on earth. Nicknamed Hell Valley after visitors were scalded to death here, it fed bathhouses below and gave the district its healing-water reputation.
s: Steaming turquoise pool nicknamed Hell Valley
why: Rare green-sulfur spring, source of Taipei's whole onsen district

w: Wood-fired since 1906, this stone-walled public sauna in the working-class Pispala district is the oldest in Finland still operating on its original site. Meter-long logs feed a stove weighing over a tonne beneath separate men's and women's rooms; regulars have queued here for a whisk-and-steam session for generations.
s: Finland's oldest wood-fired public sauna
why: Continuously operating since 1906, a living piece of sauna culture

w: Founded in 1808 by actor-turned-entrepreneur Sila Sandunov and rebuilt in palatial style in 1896, Moscow's grandest banya pairs Baroque stucco halls with wood-fired steam rooms and plunge pools once fed by a private aqueduct. Pushkin, Tolstoy and Chekhov all passed through its marble corridors on the way to the whisk.
s: 1896 marble banya loved by Tolstoy, Pushkin
why: Russia's most opulent historic bathhouse, still in daily use

w: Instead of a piazza, this Val d'Orcia hamlet centres on a medieval pool of 52C spring water, built over the Roman source that drew Lorenzo the Magnificent and Saint Catherine of Siena seeking cures. Swimming in the square pool is forbidden now, but the water runs free into rock pools at the Park of the Mills below.
s: A whole village square filled with hot water
why: Italy's only town whose main square is a thermal pool

w: Terraced geothermal pools of varying temperature climb a hillside above Fingal, tapping bore water drawn from 637 metres underground and cooled through a cascade of cave pools, a hilltop bath with 360-degree views, and a reflexology walk. Opened in 2005, it anchors Australia's largest natural hot-springs culture.
s: Terraced bore-water pools above Port Phillip
why: Australia's largest and best-known natural hot springs complex

w: Six sulfur springs rise through tectonic cracks in a limestone canyon and pool in shallow stone baths beside the arched Ottoman-era Kadiu bridge, the water settling around a mild 22-28C. Long used by shepherds for skin and joint complaints, the springs sit inside a canyon reached only by a rough gravel track.
s: Sulfur pools by an Ottoman stone bridge
why: Albania's best-known wild thermal baths, largely untouched by development

w: Brick-domed bathhouses cluster in the ravine that gave Tbilisi its name -- 'warm place' in Old Georgian -- fed by sulfurous springs drawing bathers since the fifth century. Tiled interiors and private vaulted cells, some from the 17th century, still run on the source that reputedly led a king to found the city.
s: Sulfur baths that gave Tbilisi its name
why: The founding hot spring of Georgia's capital, bathed in for 1,500 years

w: Designed in 1580 by imperial architect Sinan for an Ottoman grand admiral, this hamam carries one of his largest single domes, 17 metres high, above a marble-clad hot room ringed with private washing basins. Restored in 2012 after decades of decline, it still runs on its original wood-fired boiler system.
s: Sinan-designed 1580 hamam, a 17m dome
why: One of star architect Mimar Sinan's grandest surviving bathhouses

w: A fenced jet of mineral water erupts several metres into the air at a scalding 103C, the only active geyser on the Balkan Peninsula and among Europe's hottest springs. It sits at the edge of a small spa town otherwise built around milder pools, with Rila Monastery within easy reach.
s: The Balkans' only true erupting geyser
why: Hottest spring in Europe, the Balkans' sole active geyser

w: A bush-lined stream near the Wai-O-Tapu geothermal field cascades over shallow rock ledges into naturally warmed pools shaded by native forest, entirely free save for a car park and a short track down to the water. Named for the diesel-like sulfur smell that lingers, it is one of the last wild soaks left near Rotorua.
s: Free forest stream warmed by volcanic heat
why: Rotorua's best-loved free, undeveloped hot spring soak

w: Twice a day, for about two hours either side of low tide, geothermal water rises through the sand of an ordinary Pacific beach hot enough to dig your own spa pool with a hired spade. Two hot springs beneath the sand can reach 64C, cooled by mixing in seawater as the tide pulls back along the Coromandel coast.
s: Dig your own hot pool in the sand
why: A whole beach that becomes a DIY hot spring at low tide

w: A hike through old-growth Douglas fir leads to hand-hewn cedar tubs fed by wooden flumes from a spring first used by Native peoples and named for an 1880 prospector, Bob Bagby. Volunteers rebuilt the bathhouses after a 1979 fire, and the open-air soak remains a Pacific Northwest backcountry rite of passage.
s: Cedar tubs, a forest hike from the road
why: Oregon's classic backcountry hot spring, rebuilt by volunteers since 1981

w: An 8.5-mile trail gaining 2,500 feet ends above treeline at 11,200 feet, where mineral water surfacing at 122F pools into soaking spots ringed by 14,000-foot peaks of the Maroon Bells wilderness. A permit system now caps overnight numbers, but it remains one of the highest, most dramatic hot springs in the Rockies.
s: Alpine soak at 11,200ft below 14ers
why: One of the highest-altitude, most scenic backcountry hot springs in the US

w: Discovered by gold-mining brothers in 1905 and now powered by its own geothermal heat, this remote resort 60 miles from Fairbanks pairs a mineral-rich outdoor rock lake with some of the darkest, clearest skies for aurora viewing in North America. An ice museum carved year-round from chilled ice sits beside the springs.
s: Geothermal lake under the northern lights
why: Alaska's premier hot spring, run on its own geothermal power

w: Regarded as sacred by Tewa peoples for over a thousand years before an 1868 bathhouse made it one of America's first health resorts, this high-desert spring is unique for four distinct mineral waters -- arsenic, iron, soda and lithium -- with no sulfur smell. The 1916 hotel remains on the National Register.
s: Four unique mineral waters, no sulfur smell
why: One of America's oldest health resorts, sacred to the Tewa for centuries

w: A sweeping Art Deco crescent of white-rendered curves juts into Plymouth Sound, built in 1935 as a saltwater pool cut into the limestone shoreline below the Hoe. Closed and near-derelict by the 1990s, it was saved by a heritage campaign and restored in 2003, and now ranks among Britain's most photographed lidos.
s: 1935 Art Deco pool built into the sea cliffs
why: One of Britain's finest surviving Art Deco seawater lidos

w: Sculpted columns, carved cedar doors and zellige tilework fill this hammam attached to a 1910 pasha's palace in the Marrakech medina, among the grandest of the city's traditional bathhouses. Steam rooms of graduated heat follow the classic layout, with black-soap scrubs still given by hand on marble slabs.
s: Pasha-palace hammam of carved zellige tile
why: One of Marrakech's most architecturally lavish historic bathhouses

w: A sulfurous spring trickles down a low waterfall into shallow stone basins beside the ancient fortress ruins of Nokalakevi, an early capital of the Georgian kingdom of Egrisi. Unmarked and unheated by any resort, the pale mineral pools sit in open countryside, still used informally by locals for skin ailments.
s: Wild sulfur falls by an ancient hillfort
why: An untouched wild spring beside one of Georgia's oldest fortress sites
